source.title: Emergent Capabilities Arise Randomly from Learning Sparse Attention Patterns
source.authors: Vatsal Baherwani; Zixi Chen; Shi-Kai Qiu; Andrew Gordon Wilson; Pavel Izmailov

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream capability emergence across model scales and pre-pretraining conditions using task success and emergence timing, rather than measuring the held-out loss scaling laws themselves.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses neural scaling laws as background but does not measure held-out pretraining loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute, fit power laws, test extrapolation, or find compute-optimal allocations. Its relevant results measure task capability success and emergence timing across Pythia scales and pre-pretraining conditions. Synthetic-task training-loss results concern synthetic tasks, not the claim's held-out language-model pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: Across Pythia 14M–410M (ten seeds per scale) the paper measures whether and when four elementary capabilities emerge. Larger models acquire them earlier and more often on average. Individual capabilities, however, appear abruptly and at random training steps, and at small scales some seeds never acquire them. This bears on V6 and argues that downstream gains are predictable only as averages over seeds. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss scaling, fit any power law, or relate downstream performance to loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that capabilities emerge abruptly at random training steps and seeds, with larger models acquiring them earlier and more often on average. They attribute this to the difficulty of learning sparse attention patterns. On synthetic tasks, that difficulty is governed by context length and sparsity, and is eased by more heads or MLP-Mixer. They frame this as consistent with the quantization model, which reconciles smooth loss scaling with discrete skills. Their pre-pretraining results are described as preliminary and capability-dependent.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not fit or extrapolate scaling laws or search for compute-optimal allocations; it studies capability emergence, attention interventions, synthetic tasks, and pre-pretraining.
record.method_sensitivity: Capability emergence varies with initialization seed, task, model scale, and pre-pretraining dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Patching attention maps for K=16 causal heads into the pre-emergence checkpoint recovers most of the capability gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream capability emergence is bottlenecked by learning sparse attention patterns.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic linear-map and cellular-automata tasks: more heads lowers training loss, deeper models hurt the linear-map task, and MLP-Mixer beats the transformer on linear maps. Longer context lengthens loss plateaus multiplicatively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture shape strongly affects learning of attention-heavy synthetic tasks. This is synthetic-task training loss, not LM held-out loss.

fits_no_version.finding: At 160M, Dyck and NCA pre-pretraining tend to make in-context repetition emerge earlier, but not pattern completion (4 seeds).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Synthetic pre-pretraining can accelerate emergence of some capabilities.

record.problems: The emergence analysis uses a limited set of elementary capabilities and Pythia models below 1B parameters. The pre-pretraining experiment uses only four seeds, which the authors say limits statistical power given high inter-run variance. The paper does not report numerical uncertainty intervals for the relevant results.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant result rows were omitted. Synthetic-task training-loss and attention-pattern results were left out because they do not measure held-out language-model pretraining loss or downstream task performance as versions V1-V5 and V7 define them.

untested.parts: All; scaling laws are only cited as background.
All for language-model loss. The width, head and depth sweeps use synthetic-task training loss.
Any relation between downstream performance and pretraining loss; fitted or extrapolated downstream curves; models above 410M; benchmark suites (only single-sample elementary tasks are probed).

missing.what: Within-run abruptness: p(y*|x) stays near zero, then jumps between adjacent checkpoints. This is a result on the predictability of downstream performance across training.
Per-scale success rates and emergence steps for in-context repetition, pattern completion and IOI (rows cover only the Fig 1 task). The text says IOI is often absent in most seeds near 124M.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Its evidence on V6 is qualitative: figure-only numbers, single-sample greedy-correctness evaluation, and models below 1B parameters. The pre-pretraining rows were unlinked because they vary data rather than scale or loss.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No power-law extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token scaling.
No fixed-parameter comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details for held-out language-model loss.
No test of power-law loss scaling beyond text pretraining.
Measures capability success and emergence timing on a small set of tasks, not a general downstream benchmark suite or a fitted relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss.
No comparison of scaling-law fitting choices, exponents, or curve bending.

source_check.condition: Seed-averaged trend across Pythia 14M–410M on copying, in-context repetition, pattern completion and IOI
source_check.reason: Figures 1–2 and Section 2.3 state that larger models acquire these capabilities earlier and more often on average. The explicit ten-of-ten success result applies to copying at 160M and 410M. This supports the directional aggregate trend; no quantitative forecasting law is fitted or validated.

relationships.condition: Individual runs at a fixed scale (especially 14M–70M) and individual capabilities
relationships.reason: At a fixed scale, whether and when a capability emerges depends on the seed, and emergence is an abrupt jump at a random training step. Scale therefore predicts only averages, not single runs (R2–R4; Sec 2.1–2.3 text).
relationships.display_finding: At fixed scale, especially 14M–70M, random seeds determined whether capabilities emerged and when abrupt jumps occurred, preventing prediction of individual runs from scale alone.

source_check.condition: Individual runs at a fixed scale (especially 14M–70M) and individual capabilities
source_check.reason: Sections 2.1–2.3 report initialization-dependent success and abrupt emergence at variable training steps, qualifying predictions for individual runs. relation.reason: The Pythia experiments directly measure capability acquisition across model scales and initializations, bearing on V6.

tranche.reason: The study's own results qualify downstream predictability through seed-dependent success and abrupt, variable emergence timing despite improving average outcomes with scale.

source_check.notes: Main emergence evaluations use a single sample per task and greedy next-token correctness; Appendix A.2 finds sample-dependent emergence times. Generalization to larger models and sophisticated capabilities remains open, and calibrated seed-distribution forecasts are untested.

statements.correction: Label: limits_scope. Pythia scales: 14M, 31M, 70M, 160M, 410M; ten initializations each. Smaller scales: mixed copying success, grouped in text. 160M and 410M: all ten solve copying. Emergence timing varies across seeds; larger models acquire capabilities earlier and more often on average.
statements.problem: The study supports seed-dependent failures and abrupt emergence, but these qualify individual-run predictability rather than establish an absent or reversed aggregate scaling effect. The challenges label is inappropriate. Smaller-scale failures are reported collectively, not separately for every scale.
